title: Food & drink
description: Order food and drink, say what you do and do not eat, ask for more or less, and pay.

guide.title: Eating, drinking and the words for food
guide.text:
One verb, খাওয়া (khaaowaa), covers eating, drinking and smoking: ভাত খাই 'I eat rice', চা খাই 'I drink tea', জল খান 'have some water'.

The core of a Bengali meal: ভাত (bhaat) cooked rice; ডাল (daal) lentils; মাছ (maachh) fish; মাংস (maangsho) meat; তরকারি (torkaari) a vegetable dish or curry; রুটি (ruti) flat bread; ডিম (dim) egg; দই (doi) yogurt; মিষ্টি (mishti) sweets.

Also: জল (jol) water; চা (chaa) tea; দুধ (dudh) milk; চিনি (chini) sugar; নুন (nun) salt.

Tastes: ঝাল (jhaal) chilli-hot; মিষ্টি (mishti) sweet; টক (tok) sour; নোনতা (nontaa) salty; তেতো (teto) bitter.

নিরামিষ (niraamish) is vegetarian food; আমিষ (aamish) is fish, meat and eggs.

Bangladesh: water is পানি (paani), salt is লবণ (lobon), meat is often গোশত (gosht), and breakfast or a snack is নাস্তা (naastaa) where West Bengal says জলখাবার (jolkhaabaar).

guide.title: Asking for things
guide.text:
To order or ask, name the thing and add দিন (din) 'give': এক কাপ চা দিন। The future form দেবেন (deben) is a shade more courteous and is used for instructions about how you want something: ঝাল কম দেবেন, 'put in less chilli'.

Quantities come first: এক কাপ চা (a cup of tea), এক প্লেট ভাত (a plate of rice), দুটো রুটি (two rotis), একটু জল (a little water), আর একটু (a little more).

Note the difference: এক কাপ uses the bare number before a measure word; একটা is used when you count the things themselves.

কম (kom) is 'less' and বেশি (beshi) 'more': চিনি কম, 'less sugar'. 'Without' is ছাড়া (chhaaraa) after the noun: চিনি ছাড়া চা, 'tea without sugar'.

To refuse more food, say ব্যস (byas) 'enough' or আর লাগবে না, 'no more needed'. A good host will insist; refusing twice is normal.

examples.english: No sugar in the tea, please.

guide.title: Hungry, thirsty, full
guide.text:
You are not hungry in Bengali; hunger 'gets' you. The person is in the possessive: আমার খিদে পেয়েছে, 'my hunger has got' - I am hungry. In the same way আমার তেষ্টা পেয়েছে (aamaar teshtaa peyechhe), 'I am thirsty'.

When you have had enough: আমার পেট ভরে গেছে, 'my stomach has filled up'.

To praise the food, say it 'has turned out' well: খাবারটা খুব ভালো হয়েছে; or simply দারুণ! (daarun) 'terrific!'

আপনি খেয়েছেন? - 'Have you eaten?' - is asked out of friendliness at any time around a mealtime. It is a greeting as much as a question.

phrases.note: The first-person present works as 'let me ...'.

phrases.english: No sugar in the tea, please.
That's enough, I don't want any more.

phrases.note: Literally 'the food has turned out very well'.
A common friendly question, almost a greeting.
